name: Orange (Mandarin)
botanical: Citrus reticulata Blanco (mandarin) and the kinnow hybrid (C. nobilis × C. deliciosa)
perishability: Moderately perishable. 1–2 weeks at room temperature; 4–8 weeks at 5–8 °C.
summary: What India calls 'orange' is mostly mandarin: the Nagpur santra of Vidarbha and Malwa, the kinnow of Punjab and Rajasthan, and Khasi and Coorg mandarins in the hills. The main season runs November to March. Bangladesh is the largest export buyer, so its import duties move prices in Nagpur and Abohar.

key_numbers.label: Storage at 5–8 °C
key_numbers.note: kinnow is waxed for longer life

global: India is among the top mandarin producers. Exports (kinnow and Nagpur orange) go mainly to Bangladesh, Nepal, the Gulf and Russia. Off-season Valencia and navel oranges are imported from Egypt, South Africa, the US and Australia.

states.basis: Major producing states (ranked approximately; shares not shown)

rows.hubs: Agar Malwa, Shajapur, Rajgarh, Chhindwara (Pandhurna), Mandsaur

belts.name: Vidarbha
belts.note: Nagpur orange (GI); Warud–Morshi is the densest belt.

belts.name: Malwa
belts.note: Large Nagpur-type mandarin belt in MP and Rajasthan.

belts.name: Abohar–Fazilka–Sri Ganganagar
belts.note: Kinnow belt with waxing and grading plants.

belts.name: North-East and Coorg
belts.note: Khasi and Coorg mandarins; smaller, regional trade.

seasons.name: Nagpur ambia bahar
seasons.note: 'Sow' here means flowering. The main winter crop.

lean_season: May–September: little domestic mandarin; imports and cold-stored fruit fill shelves.

climate.v: Subtropical; needs a cool winter for colour and sugar, and a dry spell (natural or by withholding water) to trigger flowering.
13–37 °C; heat above ~40 °C causes fruit drop; frost damages kinnow in some winters.
750–1,500 mm; waterlogging spreads Phytophthora root rot.
Deep, well-drained loam, pH 5.5–7.5; Vidarbha's black soils need careful drainage.

weather_risks.impact: Mass fruit drop of the developing ambia crop and Phytophthora outbreaks.
weather_risks.example: Repeated large fruit drop in Vidarbha in wet monsoons.

weather_risks.impact: Drop of young fruit and sunburn.
Damage to flowers and the mrig crop.
Damage to kinnow fruit and young trees.

pests.name: Citrus greening (HLB)
pests.sci: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, spread by citrus psyllid
pests.impact: Incurable; trees decline over a few years.

pests.name: Phytophthora root rot and gummosis
pests.impact: Major cause of orchard decline in Vidarbha.

postharvest.respiration: Non-climacteric: harvested ripe. Ethylene 'degreening' is used only to even out peel colour.

loss.detail: Citrus as a group lost about 9.7% harvest-to-retail.

practices: Clipped (not pulled) from the tree to protect the stem end.
Kinnow is washed, waxed and graded by size in Abohar's plants; Nagpur oranges are sold by count or weight in crates.
Juice and concentrate plants (e.g. in Vidarbha) absorb lower grades.

steps.what: Many owners sell the standing crop to traders well before harvest.
Kinnow waxing plants in Abohar; manual grading in Vidarbha.
Azadpur, Kolkata, Mumbai, Bengaluru; trucks to Bangladesh via Petrapole and other border points.

supply_chain.packaging: Crates and gunny sacks (Nagpur); CFB cartons after waxing (kinnow).
supply_chain.farmer_share: Not estimated in the RBI series.

varieties.name: Kinnow
varieties.note: Juicy, seedy hybrid; the North's winter citrus.

varieties.name: Khasi mandarin, Coorg mandarin, Darjeeling mandarin
Daisy, seedless Nagpur (NRCC-4)
varieties.note: Newer introductions from ICAR-CCRI and PAU.

trade.exports: Kinnow and Nagpur orange mainly to Bangladesh; also Nepal, Bhutan, the Gulf and Russia.
trade.imports: Valencia and navel oranges from Egypt, South Africa, the US and Australia, mainly May–October.

policy.what: Bangladesh raised import duties on Indian oranges, cutting Nagpur growers' exports and prices.
Maharashtra has supported export freight and processing for Nagpur oranges.

history.what: Higher Bangladesh duties and a big crop pushed Vidarbha farm prices down.
Fruit drop cuts the ambia crop in Vidarbha.

signals: Monsoon rainfall and fruit-drop reports in Vidarbha (Jul–Sep).
Kinnow crop estimates from Punjab horticulture department (Nov).
business: The Bangladesh border trade is the swing factor for growers' prices.
Waxing, grading and cold storage add weeks of life and access to distant markets.
Off-season (May–Oct) shelves are dominated by imports: a domestic cold-store opportunity.
